title: Why the Apocrypha Is Disputed
subtitle: The books between the testaments, and why Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Bibles are different sizes.
triageNote: This is the rare page where the disagreement does not run through a single communion but between the great communions themselves. That makes it second-order in its plainest form. It divides faithful churches, not the faith. Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Christians confess the same creed and worship the same risen Lord. They carry Old Testaments of three different lengths. The dispute is old. It was argued by saints on every side. It deserves to be learned in each tradition's own voice rather than from anyone's polemics.
question: Pick up a Catholic Bible and you will find seven books a Protestant Bible lacks, Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch, and 1 and 2 Maccabees, along with longer forms of Esther and Daniel. An Orthodox Bible carries those and more, 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh, Psalm 151. Protestants call these books the Apocrypha, hidden things. Catholics call the seven deuterocanonical, belonging to a second stage of canonical recognition. The Orthodox call them anagignoskomena, things that are read. They were written by Jews, mostly between roughly 300 before Christ and the first century, mostly preserved in Greek. They circulated inside the Greek Bible the early church used. The question is whether they are Scripture. Each communion has answered with its whole history. The answers do not agree.
whyItMatters:
Practically: the first time a Protestant reads 2 Maccabees 12, where Judas Maccabeus offers sacrifice and prayer for fallen soldiers, that atonement might be made for the dead, he discovers that the line between canons and the line between doctrines run close together. Purgatory, prayer for the dead, the intercession of departed saints, all have key supports in the disputed books. That is part of why the dispute became explosive in the Reformation, when indulgences, purgatory, and 2 Maccabees arrived in the same argument. Luther disputed the book's authority at Leipzig in 1519. Trent defined the canon, including the deuterocanon, under anathema in April 1546, its first major doctrinal decree. Where you draw the table of contents has never been a merely bibliographic question.

Historically: these books are the bridge between Malachi and Matthew. The feast of Hanukkah in John 10:22 has its origin story in 1 Maccabees. The synagogue, the Pharisees and Sadducees, the Judaism Jesus moved through, took shape in the era these books narrate and breathe. Whatever you decide about their canonicity, a Christian who has never read them is a stranger to the centuries that built the world of the Gospels. That is why even the Reformers who removed them from the canon kept printing them, and kept reading them.

And personally: this page is where many readers first discover that their Bible has a history, that somebody made decisions, and that sincere Christians made them differently. That discovery can corrode trust or deepen it. The difference is usually whether someone walks you through the evidence fairly. That is what this page is for.

positions.name: The Catholic position: deuterocanonical, fully canonical
positions.inOneLine: The seven books belong to the canon of Scripture, received in the church's use from the beginning, listed by the early councils, and solemnly defined at Trent. The prefix deutero marks their history, not their rank.
positions.bestCase:
Start where the apostles started, with the Bible they actually carried. When the New Testament quotes the Old, it quotes predominantly the Greek Bible, the Septuagint. The Septuagint as the church received it carried Tobit and Judith and Wisdom and the rest within it. The oldest complete Bibles in existence, the great fourth- and fifth-century codices, Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, include these books among the Scriptures with no dividing wall. The earliest Christians did not experience a canon with an appendix. They heard Wisdom read beside Proverbs. When the second-century church met the passage in Wisdom 2, where the ungodly plot against the righteous man who calls himself a son of God, condemning him to a shameful death to test his claim, she heard the passion of Christ prophesied. She was not wrong to.

Follow the church's formal acts. When lists were drawn in the age of the councils, the councils of Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397, with Augustine present and arguing, listed these books as canonical Scripture. These are the same councils Protestants cite gladly for the New Testament canon. There is the awkwardness my separated brothers must live with. They receive the New Testament list from councils whose Old Testament list they reject. Pope Innocent I confirmed the same canon in 405. The Council of Florence repeated it in 1442, a century before Luther. So let no one tell you Trent invented the canon in a panic. In 1546 Trent defined, against a new dispute, what the church had carried for over a millennium.

Yes, Jerome demurred. We do not hide him. He is our saint too, and his preference for the Hebrew shelf, the Hebraica veritas, is part of our history. But notice three things about Jerome. He translated the disputed books anyway, under obedience. He quoted them in his other writings, sometimes with the formula as Scripture says. And the church weighed his scholarly judgment against Augustine's principle, that the usage of the universal church carries the decisive weight. She went with Augustine, as she had to. A canon is not a professor's reconstruction of Jewish opinion in the first century. It is the rule of what the church reads as God's word, and the church had been reading these books as God's word since before anyone alive could remember. As for the rabbis' narrower canon, fixed in the generations after the temple fell, I ask you honestly: why should the synagogue that did not receive Christ be the authority for the church's Old Testament, over the apostles' own Greek Bible and four centuries of Christian worship. The books are deuterocanonical, second-listed, because their road into universal recognition was longer. Their authority, now that you hold them, is not second anything.
advocates: the Councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397)

positions.name: The Orthodox position: anagignoskomena, received in the church's life
positions.inOneLine: The wider collection belongs to the church's Bible because it lives in the church's worship, received organically rather than defined juridically, profitable and read. The canon is known by life rather than by decree.
positions.bestCase:
You will notice that my Catholic brother argued like a lawyer, councils, confirmations, definitions, and I love him for it. But I want to show you another way of holding the same books. The Orthodox East never had a Trent and never needed one. Ask an Orthodox Christian where the canon is kept and he will not first hand you a conciliar decree. He will take you to Vespers. There you will hear the readings appointed for the feasts of the church, and among them, on the feasts of the martyrs, the Wisdom of Solomon: the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them. The church has sung these books for two thousand years. That is what canonical means in the East: the books that the Body of Christ, in her liturgical life, has taken into herself and made part of her breathing.

We call them anagignoskomena, the things that are read, a term from the fourth century. The term itself teaches you our mind. It is a category of practice, not of rank. Athanasius, in the same Easter letter of 367 that listed the twenty-seven New Testament books, set books like Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, and Tobit in a class of books appointed by the Fathers to be read by those newly coming to the faith. Read, in church, for formation, that is already a sacred function. The East was content for centuries to let the boundary breathe, with fathers as great as Athanasius keeping the shorter list in theory while quoting Wisdom as Scripture in practice. When the Reformation dispute finally pressed the question westward onto us, the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672 answered that books the Reformers had foolishly and ignorantly called apocrypha, Wisdom, Judith, Tobit, the Maccabees and others, are genuine parts of Scripture, because the unbroken tradition of the church had always treated them so. But notice even then, we did not anathematize a numbering system. We testified to a life.

And our shelf is wider than Rome's, 3 Maccabees, 1 Esdras, the Prayer of Manasseh, Psalm 151, which is itself instructive. The East has never felt the Western anxiety for a single, final, legally exact census of the books. For us the canon is not the foundation under the church. It is one of the treasures inside the church, kept by the same Spirit who keeps the liturgy, the icons, and the creed. The Scriptures were born in the worshiping community. They are at home in the worshiping community, and they are rightly measured there. If you ask me, then, are these books the word of God, I answer: come and stand through Holy Week, hear where the church reaches when she buries her martyrs and crowns her feasts, and you will stop asking the question as if a list could settle it. The church does not carry a Bible. The church is the place where the Bible is alive.
advocates: John of Damascus (with a narrower personal list, a tension the East holds easily)
modern Orthodox theologians such as Thomas Hopko

positions.name: The Protestant position: valuable, not canonical
positions.inOneLine: The Old Testament canon is the Hebrew canon entrusted to Israel, and the disputed books were never in it. Jesus and the apostles never cite them as Scripture. The church may read them for edification but not for doctrine.
positions.bestCase:
My case begins with a sentence of Paul: the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God. The Old Testament is, by apostolic statement, a deposit God placed with Israel. So the decisive question about its boundaries is not which books did Christians in Alexandria enjoy, but which books did the custodians receive as the oracles. And on that question the evidence speaks with unusual clarity. Josephus, around the year 95, counts a closed collection and says the succession of prophets had ended. The disputed books themselves agree. 1 Maccabees laments an age with no prophet in Israel, and the prologue to Sirach already looks back at the Law, the Prophets, and the other books as a finished inheritance the author's grandfather studied. These books know they live after prophecy. The synagogue never received them. And the church's Lord, who quarreled with the scribes over everything else, never once quarreled with them over the canon. Neither he nor his apostles ever cite one of these books with the formula it is written or Scripture says, though the New Testament quotes the Hebrew canon hundreds of times.

Now, the early church. My Catholic friend gave you Augustine and the African councils. I give you the scholars. Melito of Sardis traveled to the east around 170 specifically to learn the books of the Old Testament, and came back with the Hebrew canon, lacking the disputed books. Origen's list matches. Athanasius, in the famous letter of 367, lists the Hebrew canon and expressly sets Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, and Tobit outside it, books to be read by catechumens, not sources of doctrine, his own words. And Jerome, the one man in the ancient church who mastered Hebrew, the man the church chose to give her the Vulgate, drew the line in his prefaces around 391 to 405 with a precision the church never refuted, only outvoted: the church reads these books for the edification of the people, not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines. For edification, not for doctrine. That is not a Reformation slogan. That is the church's best scholar. The Reformers did not invent his distinction. They enforced it. Luther's 1534 Bible printed the books in a section of their own with the title: Apocrypha, that is, books which are not held equal to Holy Scripture, and yet are useful and good to read. The Thirty-Nine Articles of 1571 quote Jerome by name. The Westminster Confession of 1646 drew the conclusion in full, no authority in the church of God.

Why does the line matter so much to me. Take the test case honestly: 2 Maccabees 12 commends sacrifice and prayer for the dead, and the doctrine of purgatory leans on it. If that book is Scripture, the teaching has a footing. If it is not, a major edifice of late medieval religion, the very system of indulgences that lit the Reformation, rests on a book the church's own scholars had flagged for a thousand years. Doctrine must stand on the oracles entrusted and recognized, not on the broad and lovely margin of books the church also happened to read. I say lovely, and I mean it. Read Tobit at your fireside. Read the Maccabean martyrs and be braced. The Reformers kept these books in the Bible's back room for three centuries, and the Bible societies' decision after 1826 to stop printing them impoverished Protestant memory in ways I regret. They are the church's library. They are not the church's law.
advocates: the Thirty-Nine Articles (1571) and Westminster Confession (1646)

biblicalEvidence.summary: The Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God. The Protestant hinge: the Old Testament's boundary is set by the deposit Israel received and kept, and Israel did not keep the disputed books as Scripture.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the Catholic and Orthodox positions if entrusted means the synagogue's later judgment fixes the church's canon.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Catholic position answers that the verse describes a stewardship, not a perpetual veto, and that the Israel of the apostles included the Greek-speaking diaspora whose Bible was the wider shelf. The rabbinic canon was fixed after the church and synagogue had parted, and the church is not bound by a decision made outside her. The Orthodox add that the oracles were entrusted to be handed on, and the handing-on, to and through the church, is precisely where the wider books came in.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms. Jesus names the threefold Hebrew canon as the frame of messianic fulfillment, with no fourth shelf.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the wider-canon positions, since the Lord's own summary of the Scriptures tracks the Hebrew arrangement.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Catholic position notes that the verse describes the books that prophesy of Christ, not a census, and that Jesus also never names Esther or Ezra, which no one therefore excludes. The Orthodox observe that the church has always read Wisdom 2 as written about him. By the verse's own logic that is an argument for the book, not against it.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Judas Maccabeus has sacrifice and prayer offered for soldiers who died wearing idolatrous amulets, and the narrator commends it: therefore he made atonement for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin. The classic support for prayer for the dead and, by development, purgatory.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the Protestant position twice over. If canonical, it grounds a practice Protestantism rejects, and its rejection of the book can look doctrine-driven, the canon trimmed to fit the theology.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Protestant answer is that the order of discovery ran the other way. Jerome's line predates the purgatory debate by a millennium, and the book's canonical weakness is why doctrine should not be built there. Some add that even taken on its own terms the passage concerns idolaters awaiting resurrection, an awkward fit with developed purgatory. The Orthodox receive the passage as warrant for prayer for the dead while declining the later Latin systematization, a reminder that the same text can be received at different doctrinal depths.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The ungodly plot against the righteous man who calls God his Father and himself a child of the Lord, condemning him to a shameful death, saying God will deliver him if he is truly his son. Read by the church since the second century as a prophecy of the passion, with echoes audible in Matthew 27:43.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the Protestant position, because the passage does what canonical prophecy does, and the early church heard it that way.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Protestant reading is that the author meditates on Isaiah's suffering servant and on the perennial fate of the righteous poor, which the passion then supremely instantiates, profound, edifying, and exactly what Jerome's category was built for: read it in church, marvel, and do not seal doctrine with it. Echo, on this view, is not citation. Matthew's crowd may echo Psalm 22:8 rather than Wisdom.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Women received back their dead by resurrection, and some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life. The second clause matches no Hebrew-canon narrative and matches 2 Maccabees 7, the seven brothers tortured to death rather than apostatize, precisely.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any claim that the New Testament ignores these books entirely, since the writer to the Hebrews holds up Maccabean martyrs inside the canon's own hall of faith.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Protestant position grants the allusion cheerfully and notes what it proves: the books are known, honored history, exactly the standing Protestants give them. The chapter's same verses draw on other extracanonical traditions, Isaiah sawn in two, without canonizing their sources. Allusion to faithful history is not the formula it is written. The Catholic reply: a hall of faith whose exhibits include 2 Maccabees is a strange argument for keeping the book out of the museum.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, a caution for every side
biblicalEvidence.summary: Jude quotes the book of Enoch as prophecy and recounts a dispute over Moses' body known from the Assumption of Moses. The New Testament's use of extracanonical literature, in one short letter, and neither source was received by any of the three communions.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for everyone's simplest argument. It breaks the Protestant rule that citation marks the canon, since here citation marks books all sides exclude. And it equally breaks the Catholic-Orthodox argument from early Christian usage, since Enoch enjoyed wide early use, Tertullian defended it, and the church still let it go.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All three traditions converge on the same resolution from different directions: use, even inspired use, does not canonize a source. That is why the Protestant leans on Israel's custody, the Catholic on conciliar definition, and the Orthodox on settled liturgical reception. Each needs a principle beyond citation, and each admits, here, that the line is drawn by judgment, not by concordance.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus walks in the temple at the Feast of Dedication, Hanukkah, the festival whose origin is narrated in 1 Maccabees 4. The Lord keeps a feast whose charter document sits in the disputed books.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a Protestantism that treats the books as negligible, and useless as proof for the other side, which is what makes it instructive.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Catholics and Orthodox note, fairly, that the church's life and the disputed books are interwoven even in the Gospels. Protestants note, fairly, that observing a national feast no more canonizes 1 Maccabees than Independence Day canonizes any particular history of 1776. The verse teaches the right lesson to everyone. These books are the historical air the New Testament breathes, whatever their canonical rank.

weighing:
My judgment, offered with both hands open, because on this page I am disagreeing with whole communions either way.

I land with Jerome, and therefore with the Protestant line. The reason is Romans 3:2 read beside the evidence of Josephus, the Sirach prologue, and the New Testament's citation pattern. The Old Testament canon was a deposit entrusted to Israel. The custodians kept a defined shelf. The disputed books themselves remember an age after prophecy, and the apostles, who quote the Hebrew canon by the hundreds, never once seal a doctrine with it is written from the books in dispute. When the one ancient Christian scholar who could read the custodians' language drew his line, for edification, not for doctrine, I think he read the situation rightly. And I notice his line held even inside the medieval church, where figures as central as Gregory the Great and Cardinal Cajetan, Luther's own examiner, could still repeat it.

But I want to say two things against my own side, because fairness demands them and so does the evidence. First, the Catholic argument from the councils has a real grip. A Protestant who receives the New Testament canon from the discernment of the fourth-century church, as I do, cannot wave away that same church's Old Testament lists as mere error without explaining himself. My explanation is Jerome, the contemporary dissent of the church's best-equipped scholar, preserved and honored within the tradition itself. The New Testament list had no Jerome. You may judge whether that carries the weight I place on it. Second, the Orthodox have hold of something Protestants keep forgetting. Canon is not only a boundary. It is a life, and the books that nourished the martyrs are not nothing. The decision after 1826 to print Bibles with the back room emptied was a quiet vandalism. The average Protestant's total ignorance of the Maccabees is not a victory for sola scriptura. It is a hole in the family memory.

So: I do not preach from Tobit, and I will not ground doctrine east of Malachi and west of Matthew. And the copy of the Apocrypha on my shelf is worn, and I commend the same to you, read as the Reformers read it, profitably, gratefully, and without the formula it is written.
charitableDisagreement:
Name what each communion is guarding and the heat drops at once. The Catholic is guarding the principle that Christ left a church able to settle what binds the faithful. Without it, he will tell you plainly, you do not finally have a canon at all, only opinions about one. The Orthodox is guarding the unity of Scripture and worship, a Bible that lives in the liturgy rather than under a magnifying glass. The Protestant is guarding the purity of doctrine's foundation, the conviction that what the church teaches must rest on what God demonstrably gave. His narrower shelf is not stinginess. It is fear of God. Three loves, three architectures, one Lord.

Is it a hill to die on. The Reformers and Trent thought so, and anathemas flew in both directions. It is not for me to pretend the sixteenth century was a misunderstanding. The doctrines downstream, purgatory above all, are real disagreements with real pastoral consequences, and they deserve their own pages and their own seriousness. But hear the proportions. Every book in dispute lies between the testaments. No article of the creed rests there. The three communions that divide over these books confess together the Trinity, the incarnation, the cross, the resurrection, and the judgment, all from the books they share. If you are Protestant, read the Apocrypha before you dismiss men who die rather than break the law of God in 2 Maccabees 7. If you are Catholic or Orthodox, understand that the Protestant's narrower canon was drawn by the church's own greatest Hebraist, in love for the same Scriptures. And whoever you are, do not let a dispute about the books between the testaments keep you from the Christ to whom both testaments point.

relatedDebates.topic: How we got the Old Testament
relatedDebates.note: The prior page of this set. Whether the Hebrew canon was closed before these books could enter it is half of this entire dispute. The three positions there map closely onto the three communions here.

relatedDebates.topic: Purgatory and prayer for the dead
relatedDebates.note: The doctrinal stakes of 2 Maccabees 12 in concentrated form. Whether the faithful departed can be helped by the prayers of the living divides the communions along nearly the same line as the canon question. The two disputes have reinforced each other since 1519.

Underneath the canon question sits the authority question: whether Scripture alone norms doctrine, or Scripture within tradition, or Scripture and tradition together. Each communion's answer to this page is its answer to that one, applied to a list of books.
